sources: M1 clock and flash implementation reviews

title: Clock and boot decisions
body: The selected oscillator is 125 MHz LVDS at 1.8 V. M1 keeps the AC-coupling pair and uses a supplier-derived land pattern.
M1 omits the LMK splitter while the GTP ODIV2 fabric-clock path awaits Vivado verification.
The original slide asks for better than ±20 ppm but lists a ±25 ppm oscillator. That requirement still needs reconciliation.
The 1.8 V flash crosses the 1.5 V FPGA configuration interface through NVT4858. SPI x1 boot and brownout behavior need testing.
notes: The oscillator fits the reference-clock interface as a prototype selection. Its quoted 186 fs jitter was characterized at 3.3 V, so it does not settle the 1.8 V clock qualification. We need to verify the internal fabric-clock route and resolve the ppm mismatch. NVT4858 comes from an SD/SDIO application, and the implemented SPI adaptation still requires physical boot checks. RMS phase jitter also does not verify the slide’s peak-to-peak cycle-to-cycle jitter requirement. The proposed LMK exact-part hyperlink differs from the typed suffix and needs checking if later fitted.

title: Simpler ASIC connections
body: M1 removes all 15 ASIC bus buffers and 56 parts overall. The component count falls from 343 to 287.
The original same-ASIC LDO and ECP5 reference circuits connect their digital signals directly.
M1 retains the outgoing 33 Ω damping arrays, passive defaults, boot holds and stimulation permission logic.
Removing buffers also removes their powered-off isolation. Controlled power sequencing and interface qualification remain necessary.
foot: All 116 ASIC paths pass independent connectivity checks. Twenty-two receive-default arrays remain fitted.
notes: The references support trying direct nominal 1.5 V signaling. Recording returns remain individual wires. Shared outgoing controls can have heavier loads as we scale to eight ASICs. We should add a targeted driver only where load or edge evidence supports it. We have not removed the 22 receive-default arrays or replaced them with a verified firmware policy. Native ERC, physical DRC and parity are zero, with PCB routing still open.

title: Gerald’s board-design guidance
body: Place repeated circuits clearly, following signal flow and short local power loops.
Match total clock/data timing within each related I/O group. Shorten detours before tuning.
Keep continuous ground references and deliberate return connections at layer changes. Place bypass capacitors at their ICs.
Use manufacturable FPGA escapes. Gerald’s 1–2, 1–3 and 1–4 blind-via spans need a fabricator-approved construction.
Keep necessary functions in a compact placement, with bottom mezzanine connectors and a clear overall schematic.
notes: The October 6 feedback highlighted routing quality, regular placement and unmatched delays. The earlier directions also call for power-distribution checks, practical blind-via escapes, compact placement and bottom connectors. Our engineering application is to review the full signal and return path, not only visual symmetry. A factory stackup and guaranteed ASIC timing still need evidence.
sources: 6 October recorded Gerald feedback and routing plan

title: Existing ASIC LDO board
foot: Nine regulator/reference stages. J1/J19 housing models are absent. J19 has no assigned nets. Installed population remains unverified.
notes: This is Gerald’s existing LDO design. Its 23 digital signals pass directly between the connectors. The rail intents include separate nominal 1.5 V domains, 1.6 V, 0.75 V and two high-stage circuits. The high-stage sign and reference must stay explicit. All nine LDO power-good outputs are unused in the saved circuit, so a raw-input monitor does not establish that every ASIC rail is ready. Actual fitted parts, currents, return bonding and power order remain to be checked.

title: Received direct-carrier layout
foot: Board_Howard draft: 38 DRC errors, 21 dangling-track warnings and 20 assigned open connections. Compare with saved Step 8.
notes: The new Desktop package contains the connector-foundation carrier. Show where the LDO and XEM sockets sit and how the recording bus runs between them. Do not call this a complete powered carrier. The older R3 and R5 circuits remain different revisions, and the R3 manufacturing hold remains in place. The received board uses two copper layers and has no ground plane. The saved Step 8 uses four copper layers and a dedicated In1.Cu DGND plane.

foot: Native preview includes the Samtec XEM sockets. Hirose J1/J19 housings are missing. Seating and assembled fit remain open.

title: Carrier routing status
foot: Step 8 returned data/clock geometry: 48.547–63.830 mm, 15.283 mm spread. This measurement belongs to the saved baseline.
notes: The new Desktop draft has changed copper and needs review before replacing the applied Step 8 baseline. Fresh native checks report 59 native DRC findings: 38 errors and 21 dangling-track warnings, 20 assigned unconnected items and 204 parity warnings. The same parity total does not mean every entry is the same. Step 8’s 234 unassigned contacts were checked independently, and its 204 parity warnings remain recorded. Neither set of checks establishes complete timing or a powered carrier. The 15.283 mm spread describes only the saved baseline and has no accepted skew threshold.
sources: 6 October Step 8 native and independent checks

title: Next review decisions
body: Confirm the FPGA clock path, oscillator tolerance and SPI boot behavior for the selected parts.
Review the compact placement and carrier routing with Gerald, then route against an explicit timing and return-path plan.
Close ASIC pad limits, per-rail loads, power order and shared-control loading before operating the direct interface.
Check simultaneous connector mating, actual component bodies and the manufacturer’s stackup before fabrication.
Build the matched FPGA/host workflow and test one ASIC before assessing eight-chip operation.
notes: Our next concrete review should use the native two-sheet FPGA drawing and the new carrier PCB. The requirements that still need ASIC-side evidence are pad levels, recording data-valid timing, rail currents and power-loss behavior. The fabrication stackup and mechanical seating need supplier or physical evidence. The one-chip XEM path is the first integration step, with eight-chip scaling following verified results.
sources: Carrier manufacturing hold and routing plan
